$comment: PhotoCraft's Erasmus manifest. Copy this to erasmus-packages/manifests/photocraft.json when
publishing; see PUBLISHING.md there and docs/erasmus.md here for the design behind every
choice below.
A manifest is DATA, validated against Erasmus's shared/schema/manifest.ts and nothing else.
Everything only a build can know -- install.artifacts' url, byte count and sha256, and the
icon's asset url -- is left out: the private-repository tier does not read a manifest's claim
about where to download itself from. Erasmus fills those in from the release and from the line
in packages.txt that a person wrote and git recorded.
WHY THE PORT IS 'allocated' AND NOT 'fixed'. The publishing guide's checklist says to declare
'fixed' matching your program's own default port, and records a real bug where 'allocated'
defeated a sibling program's deliberate discoverability. That reasoning does not transfer:
PhotoCraft has no default control port at all. Its --control <port> is required and
user-chosen by design, so there is nothing for 'fixed' to match and nothing for 'allocated'
to defeat -- and 'allocated' additionally lets two PhotoCraft windows run at once, which an
image editor is asked for more often than a CAD kernel is.
WHY THE TOKEN IS 'generated' AND NOT 'handshake'. 'handshake' exists for a program that must
persist its own credential so a URL registered with some external MCP client keeps working
across restarts. Nothing holds a saved PhotoCraft bridge URL, so a credential minted fresh per
launch is both sufficient and the shorter-lived of the two.
WHY THERE IS A HANDSHAKE FILE ANYWAY. It carries three things only the running program knows,
none of which is the port or the token: its window handle (so window.match can be 'handshake',
the one exact strategy -- a title match on 'PhotoCraft' would happily attach to a copy the user
already had open, which for an image editor is the normal case and not a corner one), the
directory its logs are in (read on exit, when the runtime directory is about to be swept), and
its own longest real tool budget.
WHY callTimeoutMs IS FIVE MINUTES. docs/scorecard.md measures what PhotoCraft's slow
operations actually cost on a large document: ~3.4s to save a 36 MP layered PSD, ~3.1s for a
Gaussian blur, ~9.9s for a full refresh of a 14000x14000 document. The 30s default would be
fine for those and wrong for Content-Aware Scale, which is currently measured at 954s against
a 3s budget (photocraft #211). The failure a short budget produces is the worst shape
available: the host gives up, the model is told the call failed, and PhotoCraft carries on and
commits the edit anyway. The number here is a FLOOR -- the program publishes its real budget
through handshake.callTimeoutField and the host raises its own wait to match.
WHAT `opens` CLAIMS, AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT. The layered and native formats
(psd, psb, pcraft), the two PhotoCraft handles specially (tif, exr) and camera raw are all
cases where PhotoCraft is plainly the right thing to hand a file to. The flat web formats --
png, jpg, gif, webp -- are not here on purpose: PhotoCraft opens them, but so does everything
else on the machine, and claiming them makes PhotoCraft the default opener for every image
mentioned in a transcript. That is a product decision rather than a technical one, and adding
them is a one-line change whenever it is made. `tool` is always the literal `open_file`: the
point of fixing the name is that a host which has matched an extension never has to look up
what this program called its own opener.
There is no `skillPath` -- PhotoCraft serves only the structured /skills document, and two
documents saying the same thing is two documents to keep in sync.
install.stripPrefix is omitted on purpose, which is not the same as forgotten. The portable
zip has exactly one top-level directory and it IS a packaging wrapper
(photocraft-<version>-windows-<arch>-portable/), so the install pipeline's own heuristic --
promote a single top-level directory -- is correct here. Naming it explicitly would mean
transcribing a version number into this file on every release for no gain.
WHY install.keep NAMES PhotoCraftData. portable.txt beside photocraft.exe is the whole reason
verifyFiles lists it: it switches PhotoCraft into portable mode, so preferences, brush presets
and crash-recovery autosaves live in PhotoCraftData INSIDE the install root instead of
%APPDATA%. That is the right shape for a hosted program -- an uninstall takes the install root
and leaves nothing behind -- but an update finishes with one atomic rename INTO that same
install root, so without `keep` every update would quietly discard the user's settings and
presets. `keep` hard-links the tree across from the previous install (carryOver.ts walks a
directory and links each file), which is exactly what this field exists for. First install has
no previous version and reports `no-source`, which is harmless.
uninstall.warnPaths names %APPDATA%\Photocraft and nothing else because that is genuinely the
only place PhotoCraft can write outside its install root: app_dirs::resolve falls back to it
when portable mode is on but PhotoCraftData is not writable (a read-only drive). There is no
second cache or scratch location to warn about.
label: PhotoCraft
summary: Layered image editing with real PSD files, in a native app written entirely in Rust.
description:
PhotoCraft is an image editor with Photoshop-comparable behaviour and file fidelity, written entirely in Rust. Layers, masks, adjustment layers, layer styles, type, vectors and brushes, with a GPU compositor on wgpu and multithreaded filters.

It opens, edits and saves real layered Photoshop documents, reads camera raw from most major makers, and keeps anything it does not model yet verbatim rather than dropping it. Its own .pcraft format is lossless and incremental.

Every user-visible action is a command with an id, which is what makes the whole editor drivable: the menus, the CLI, the JSON control channel and this bridge all dispatch the same commands. That is also why the tool list here is short and its reach is not -- command_list finds any of them and command_run performs it.
